newsitem.title: GREECE: New Greek PM vows to fight tax fraud, cut spending.
newsitem.headline: New Greek PM vows to fight tax fraud, cut spending.

text.p: Greece's newly-elected socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis vowed on Thursday to fight rampant tax evasion, cut government spending and do away with tax breaks for the wealthy in his first major economic policy speech.
Addressing the new parliament, he warned deputies there was "no magic wand" which would allow the European Union's poorest state to solve its economic woes without paying a price.
In a clear shot across the bows of the wealthy ahead of the 1997 budget, he noted: "Especially those who have must give."
The basic targets of his economic policy would be to lower inflation and state deficits while accelerating growth, he said.
Simitis, 60, took over as prime minister in January. He was elected to a four-year term in snap elections last month and has 162 deputies in the 300-seat parliament.

A trained economist and lawyer, Simitis has signalled he is a new, fiscally responsible socialist. He has turned his back on the wild free-spending populism of his predecessor -- the late Andreas Papandreou -- which nearly bankrupted the country.
Simitis's first challenge will be shaping the 1997 budget, due next month, so that it can meet strict economic targets set out in the EU's Maastricht treaty.

He gave no details of how he would cut stubborn inflation, 8.5 percent year-on-year in August. Inflation fell to single digits in 1995 for the first time in 22 years but it has proved resilient to efforts to push it down much further.
Simitis said Greece's biggest problem was its chronic budget deficits which have helped swell the total public debt to more than 110 percent of GDP.
"Let us not forget that the interest alone which the state pays (on its debt) is more than combined spending on defence, education, health and social security," he said.

Simitis stressed that getting Greece's fiscal house in order was "a basic condition for our participation in EU decision making." An initial indication of his sincerity will come with the 1997 budget -- the first he will oversee as prime minister.
He said that the goal of his government would be to meet EU convergence targets and fulfil conditions for joining EU Economic and Monetary Union by the year 2000.
"Greece ... will be judged in coming years by its participation in the EMU. It is our firm decision to fulfil the requirements of joining EMU by the end of the decade," he said.
To help meet EU economic criteria, his government would:
-- contain state waste and take advantage of state properties. State spending must correspond to the real needs of society.

-- stop the perpetuation of preferential tax treatment that increases social inequality and "has no place in a modern and just tax system." But he would not cut all deductions which have "social justification or help growth."
-- intensify the fight against tax evasion and the black economy. He pledged the "just distribution of costs on all social classes."
The vast black economy, which dodges all taxation, is estimated at 35 to 40 percent of Greece's annual $110 billion GDP.
Simitis said his government would quickly present draft bills to cut state spending and tax deductions, and to reform customs codes and fight smuggling.
